families.name: Bantu
families.description: Largest language family in Kenya (~65% of population). Spread across central, western, and coastal regions.

families.name: Nilotic
families.description: Second largest family (~30%). Includes Plains Nilotes (Maasai), Highland Nilotes (Kalenjin), and River-Lake Nilotes (Luo).

families.name: Cushitic
families.description: Found in northern and eastern Kenya (~3%). Includes Somali, Rendille, Oromo, and Borana.

families.name: Other
families.description: Includes Swahili (Bantu-based lingua franca), English (official), and minor language isolates.

languages.name: Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ)
languages.notes: Largest ethnic group. Central highlands.

languages.name: Dholuo (Luo)
languages.notes: River-Lake Nilotes. Lake Victoria basin.

languages.name: Kalenjin
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes. Several sub-groups: Nandi, Kipsigis, Tugen, Pokot, Marakwet, Sabaot.

languages.name: Luhya (Luyia)
languages.notes: 17+ dialects including Bukusu, Maragoli, Idakho, Isukha, Tiriki.

languages.name: Kamba (Kĩkamba)
languages.notes: Eastern province. Known for wood carving and music.

languages.name: Somali
languages.notes: Dominant in North Eastern. Cross-border with Somalia.

languages.name: Kisii (Ekegusii)
languages.notes: Kisii Highlands. Known for soapstone carving.

languages.name: Meru (Kĩmĩĩrũ)
languages.notes: Mt. Kenya eastern slopes. Several sub-dialects.

languages.name: Maasai (Maa)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes. Pastoralist culture. Samburu is a closely related dialect.

languages.name: Turkana (Ng'aturukana)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Eastern Nilotic). Semi-nomadic pastoralists. Spoken across Turkana County in northwestern Kenya. Rich pastoralist vocabulary and oral traditions.

languages.name: Embu (Kĩembu)
languages.notes: Mt. Kenya southeastern slopes. Related to Kikuyu and Meru.

languages.name: Taita (Kidawida)
languages.notes: Taita Hills. Three main dialects: Dawida, Sagala, Kasigau.

languages.name: Swahili (Kiswahili)
languages.notes: National & official language. Native along the coast but spoken nationwide as lingua franca.

languages.name: Mijikenda
languages.notes: Nine sub-groups: Giriama, Digo, Duruma, Chonyi, Jibana, Kambe, Ribe, Rabai, Kauma.

languages.name: Borana (Oromo)
languages.notes: Cushitic pastoralists. Related to Ethiopian Oromo.

languages.name: Rendille
languages.notes: Camel-herding pastoralists. Unique language between Somali and Afar.

languages.name: Teso (Ateso)
languages.notes: Cross-border with Uganda. Part of the broader Teso ethnic group.

languages.name: Pokomo
languages.notes: Tana River farmers. One of the smaller Bantu groups.

languages.name: Samburu
languages.notes: Closely related to Maasai. Semi-nomadic pastoralists.

languages.name: Ilchamus (Njemps)
languages.notes: Lake Baringo fishermen/farmers. Related to Maasai/Samburu. Endangered language.

languages.name: Pokot (Pökoot)
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Northern Kalenjin branch). Pastoralists and terrace farmers in West Pokot and Baringo counties; documented in Mervyn Beech's 1911 monograph.

languages.name: Taveta (Kitaveta)
languages.notes: Northeast Coast Bantu (Pare-Taveta group) spoken around Taveta and Lake Jipe; rich oral proverb tradition documented by A. C. Hollis (1910).

officialLanguages.use: Government, judiciary, higher education, formal business
Everyday communication, National Assembly, primary education, media

notes: Kenya has 42+ recognized ethnic groups speaking 60+ distinct languages and dialects.
Speaker numbers are estimates based on KNBS 2019 Census ethnic population data (language ≈ ethnicity for most groups).
County-level language dominance is approximate. Urban areas (especially Nairobi, Mombasa) are highly multilingual.
Several Kenyan languages are classified as endangered by UNESCO, including El Molo (~300 speakers), Yaaku, Suba, and Omotik.
Data compiled from KNBS 2019 Census and UNESCO Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger.
source: Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 Population and Housing Census & Constitution of Kenya
